title: From Call Flows to Autonomous Agents: Building Real-Time Voice AI with Twilio + LiveKit

body:
For years, voice bots were just IVRs with better NLP rigid flows, brittle logic, and zero real understanding. In this deep technical case study, I break down how I rebuilt my entire voice and SMS automation stack using Twilio, LiveKit, and agentic AI pipelines to create real-time agents that listen, reason, interrupt, and act across channels and what it actually takes to make them work in production.

The End of Scripted Voice Bots

For most of the last decade, “AI voice automation” meant one thing: IVR trees wrapped in NLP.

Press 1 for sales.
Press 2 for support.
Say “billing” to hear your balance.

Even when we added intent classifiers or FAQ bots, the architecture stayed the same:

User speaks → system maps to intent → system returns a fixed response → wait for next turn.

These systems could answer questions, but they couldn’t own workflows. They couldn’t plan. They couldn’t recover gracefully when users interrupted them. They couldn’t coordinate actions across voice, SMS, CRM, and backend systems.

They were reactive responders, not goal-driven agents.

That changed for me when I started building a real-time voice + SMS agentic pipeline using Twilio and LiveKit one agent brain, multiple channels, real autonomy, real workflows.

This article walks through:

  • Why traditional Twilio IVR architectures break down in modern AI systems
  • What an agentic AI pipeline actually looks like in production
  • How Twilio + LiveKit enable real-time voice agents that feel human
  • The hardest engineering problems (latency, barge-in, state, observability)
  • Pseudo-code and architecture patterns you can copy into real systems

This isn’t hype. This is what it actually takes to build production-grade real-time voice AI agents in 2026.

Before Agentic AI: How Voice & SMS Systems Actually Worked

Let’s be honest about how most Twilio voice bots and SMS systems were built.

Typical Pre-Agentic Architecture

  • Twilio phone number / SMS number
  • TwiML or webhook flows
  • Hard-coded IVR menu
  • Regex or intent-classifier routing
  • Separate logic for voice, SMS, chat

Flow looked like:

User → Twilio → Webhook → Intent Classifier → Response → Wait

Each turn was stateless or lightly stateful. The system never “owned” the session it just reacted.

Even when LLMs arrived, many systems simply replaced the intent classifier with GPT:

User → GPT → Response → Wait

Still not agentic. Still reactive.

What These Systems Couldn’t Do

They struggled with:

  • Multi-step workflows (“schedule, confirm, follow up”
  • Cross-channel continuity (voice → SMS → outbound call)
  • Interruptions and natural speech dynamics
  • Long-lived task tracking
  • Autonomous decision-making

If the user changed their mind mid-call, the system broke.

If the call dropped and continued over SMS, the context was lost.

If the agent needed to proactively call the user later, there was no concept of planning or delayed actions.

This is where agentic AI pipelines fundamentally change the architecture.

What Agentic AI Adds (Without the Buzzwords)

Agentic systems aren’t just “LLMs with tools.” They represent a shift in how we structure software.

Three properties define them:

1. Autonomy

The system decides the next step.

Not:

“If intent == X, do Y.”

But:

“Given the user’s goal and current state, what should I do next?”

2. Goal Orientation

Instead of responding to turns, the agent works toward outcomes:

  • Qualify the lead
  • Resolve the issue
  • Reschedule the appointment
  • Recover a failed payment
  • Reduce abandonment

The conversation is no longer the product, the outcome is.

3. Action Layer

The agent doesn’t just talk. It:

  • Calls APIs
  • Sends SMS
  • Updates CRMs
  • Schedules events
  • Triggers workflows
  • Makes outbound calls later

This is what turns LLMs from chatbots into workflow engines.

Now combine that with:

  • Twilio → reliable global telephony + SMS rails
  • LiveKit → real-time low-latency audio streaming

And you get something very different from “chatbot with a phone number.”

You get real-time voice agents that perceive, reason, and act continuously across channels under strict latency and UX constraints.

The Mental Model Shift: From Request, Response to Continuous Control Loops

Traditional voice bots operate in discrete turns.

Agentic voice systems operate as continuous control loops:

Perceive → Reason → Act → Observe → Adapt → Repeat

In a real-time Twilio + LiveKit pipeline, this becomes:

  1. Perceive
  • Capture live audio stream
  • Perform streaming STT
  • Track speech boundaries, silence, barge-in

2. Reason

  • Update conversation + user state
  • Run agent planner over current context
  • Decide next action(s)

3. Act

  • Speak via TTS
  • Send SMS
  • Call APIs
  • Trigger workflows
  • Schedule follow-ups

4. Observe

  • Listen for interruption
  • Monitor tool outcomes
  • Detect errors, latency, confusion

This loop runs continuously, not per turn.

That’s the difference between a chatbot and a voice operating system.

Real Project: Building a Twilio + LiveKit Agentic Voice & SMS System

In my current project, the goal was deceptively simple:

“Let one AI agent handle inbound support calls, follow up with outbound calls when needed, and send SMS confirmations all with one brain, not three separate bots.”

Stack Overview

  • Twilio
  • Inbound and outbound calls
  • SMS
  • SIP trunking
  • Call routing
  • LiveKit
  • Real-time audio streaming
  • Barge-in detection
  • Low-latency media transport
  • STT
  • Whisper / Deepgram / AssemblyAI (depending on latency vs accuracy tradeoffs)
  • TTS
  • ElevenLabs / Azure / Google (depending on voice quality vs speed)
  • LLM
  • OpenAI GPT-4.x or Anthropic Claude in an agentic orchestration layer
  • Backend
  • Session manager
  • State store
  • Tool interfaces (CRM, scheduling, SMS, analytics)

High-Level Flow

  1. Inbound call hits Twilio number
  2. Twilio routes audio into LiveKit via SIP or media stream
  3. LiveKit streams audio frames to backend
  4. Backend performs STT → agent reasoning → TTS
  5. Audio response streams back through LiveKit → Twilio → caller
  6. Agent optionally sends SMS, schedules follow-ups, or triggers outbound calls

This is not a stateless webhook flow.

This is a long-lived, stateful, real-time agent loop controlling voice interactions.

  • Twilio → LiveKit → Agent Backend
  • STT, LLM Agent, TTS layers
  • Tool integrations (CRM, Scheduler, SMS, Analytics)
  • Outbound call + SMS paths

The Four Engineering Problems That Actually Matter

Once you move from scripted flows to real-time agentic voice systems, four problems dominate everything else:

  1. Latency
  2. Barge-in & interruptions
  3. Cross-channel state
  4. Observability

Let’s walk through each at production depth.

1. Latency: The Invisible System Killer

In chat apps, 2–3 seconds of latency is annoying but acceptable.

In voice, anything over ~700 ms feels broken.

Latency compounds:

  • Audio capture
  • Network hop to STT
  • STT inference
  • Agent reasoning
  • TTS synthesis
  • Audio streaming back

If you’re careless, you end up with:

  • Robotic pacing
  • Users interrupting constantly
  • Awkward silences
  • Loss of trust within seconds

Latency Budgeting (Real Numbers)

In production, I treat each turn like a real-time system budget:

ComponentTargetAudio chunking + transport~50 msSTT streaming partials~100–200 msAgent reasoning~150–300 msTTS synthesis~100–200 msAudio playback buffer~50–100 ms

Total target: ~450–800 ms per turn.

That’s hard. But achievable with the right architecture.

What Actually Worked

  1. Streaming STT
  • Use streaming transcription APIs (Deepgram / AssemblyAI / Whisper streaming variants)
  • Start reasoning before the user finishes speaking

2. Incremental LLM generation

  • Use token streaming where possible
  • Begin TTS synthesis before full response completes

3. Short prompts, small context windows

  • Move memory into structured state stores
  • Feed LLM only what it needs for the current decision

4. Faster voices over prettier voices

  • ElevenLabs and Azure Neural voices vary wildly in synthesis latency
  • For real-time systems, choose voices that synthesize in <150 ms

5. Avoid unnecessary network hops

  • Run STT, agent, and TTS in the same region
  • Keep Twilio → LiveKit → backend path minimal

Latency is not a tuning problem it’s an architecture constraint.

  • STT latency
  • LLM inference
  • TTS synthesis
  • Network hops
  • Total turn time

2. Barge-In: Humans Interrupt Your Agent Must Survive That

Humans don’t wait politely for bots to finish speaking.

They interrupt. They correct. They clarify mid-sentence.

Early versions of my system failed badly here:

  • TTS kept playing while user talked
  • Agent ignored interruption
  • Response arrived to something the user said 5 seconds ago
  • Conversation derailed instantly

This is the difference between a demo bot and a real voice agent.

What Barge-In Actually Requires

You need:

  1. Real-time audio energy detection
  2. Immediate cancellation of TTS playback
  3. Agent plan invalidation
  4. High-priority reprocessing of new utterance

This turns your agent into a preemptive state machine, not a turn-based chatbot.

How I Implemented It

  • LiveKit provides real-time audio frame events.
  • When inbound speech energy crosses a threshold:
  • Stop or fade out TTS playback
  • Cancel current agent plan
  • Flush partial reasoning context
  • Inject new utterance as high-priority input

The agent is not “mid-turn” anymore.

It’s mid-control-loop, and must adapt instantly.

This alone eliminates 80% of the uncanny valley in voice AI.

  • User speaking
  • STT partials
  • Agent planning
  • TTS start
  • User interrupts
  • TTS cancelle
  • New reasoning loop begins

3. State and Memory Across Voice + SMS Channels

Users do not care that:

  • Voice uses WebRTC
  • SMS uses HTTP webhooks
  • Outbound calls use Twilio call SID callbacks

They expect continuity.

They expect:

  • “Yes, that’s what I just told you on the phone.”
  • “Why are you asking again? I confirmed already.”

This breaks almost every naive architecture.

Failure Modes I Hit

  • Voice agent resolved half the issue, SMS follow-up forgot everything.
  • Outbound call didn’t know the user had already confirmed by text.
  • LLM hallucinated previous context because state wasn’t centralized.

The Solution: Centralized Conversation State

The agent must never rely solely on LLM context.

Instead:

  • Every session has:
  • User profile state
  • Conversation history summary
  • Task progress
  • Tool side effects
  • Pending actions

This lives in:

  • Redis / DynamoDB / Postgres / KV store
  • Versioned per session and per user
  • Read and written by the agent on every step

Voice and SMS are just views into the same agent brain.

That’s how you get continuity across:

  • Inbound calls
  • SMS replies
  • Outbound follow-ups
  • Delayed workflows

4. Observability: Is This Agent Actually Working?

Voice agents feel magical when they succeed and inscrutable when they fail.

Without deep observability, you’re blind.

What You Must Log

At minimum:

  • Raw STT outputs
  • Final transcripts
  • Agent decisions
  • Tool calls and results
  • TTS outputs
  • Latency at every stage
  • Errors, retries, fallbacks

What You Must Measure

  • Call containment rate (no human escalation)
  • Task success rate
  • Average call duration
  • Interruption frequency
  • Latency percentiles
  • User sentiment (if available)

Why This Matters

Without this:

  • You don’t know if your agent is improving outcomes or just sounding fluent.
  • You can’t debug failures.
  • You can’t safely deploy changes.
  • You can’t scale.

With it:

  • You tune prompts based on real failure patterns.
  • You optimize tools that cause confusion.
  • You detect regressions immediately.

Agentic voice systems require production-grade observability, not demo metrics.

  • STT → Agent → Tool calls → TTS
  • Logged at each step with timestamps
  • Metrics overlay

Core Architecture: The Agentic Control Loop

Now let’s look at what this system actually looks like structurally.

Forget frameworks for a moment.

At its core, an agentic voice system is:

while (session.active):
    perceive()
    reason()
    act()
    observe()

The important shift is:

  • The agent owns the loop.
  • The agent owns the state.
  • The agent decides when the loop ends.

Not the webhook.
Not the user turn.
Not the IVR flow.

The agent.

Pseudo-Code: Real-Time Voice Agent Loop (Twilio + LiveKit)

Below is conceptual TypeScript-style pseudo-code capturing the production pattern. This is not framework-specific it’s architectural.

// High-level agent loop for a real-time Twilio + LiveKit voice session
async function handleVoiceSession(session: SessionContext) {
  const stream = session.livekitStream;
  while (session.isActive) {
    // 1. Perception: wait for speech input
    const audioChunk = await stream.waitForUserSpeech();
    // 2. STT (streaming preferred)
    const transcript = await sttService.transcribe(audioChunk);
    // Load persistent state (not from LLM memory)
    const state = await loadConversationState(session.userId);
    // 3. Reasoning: agent decides next step
    const agentResult = await agent.decide({
      userId: session.userId,
      channel: "voice",
      transcript,
      state,
      tools: {
        sms: sendSmsViaTwilio,
        crm: updateCrmRecord,
        schedule: scheduleAppointment,
        outboundCall: placeOutboundCall,
      },
    });
    // Persist updated state
    await saveConversationState(session.userId, agentResult.updatedState);
    // 4. Actions
    // Voice reply
    if (agentResult.voiceReply) {
      const audio = await ttsService.synthesize(agentResult.voiceReply);
      await stream.play(audio);
    }
    // Optional SMS follow-up
    if (agentResult.smsToSend) {
      await sendSmsViaTwilio({
        to: session.userPhone,
        body: agentResult.smsToSend,
      });
    }
    // Optional outbound call scheduling
    if (agentResult.scheduleOutboundCall) {
      await placeOutboundCall(agentResult.callDetails);
    }
    // Human escalation
    if (agentResult.shouldEscalateToHuman) {
      await transferCallToHuman(session.twilioCallSid);
      break;
    }
    // Session termination
    if (agentResult.shouldEndSession) {
      await stream.end();
      break;
    }
  }
}

Key properties of this loop:

  • Single agent brain across channels
  • Explicit state management
  • Tool calls as first-class actions
  • Interruptible
  • Observable

This is not request–response.

This is continuous control.

Pseudo-Code: SMS Agent Loop (Same Brain, Different Interface)

SMS uses the same agent, same state, same tools just a different transport.

async function handleSmsWebhook(req, res) {
  const { from, body } = req.twilioPayload;
  const state = await loadConversationState(from);
  const agentResult = await agent.decide({
    userId: from,
    channel: "sms",
    transcript: body,
    state,
    tools: {
      sms: sendSmsViaTwilio,
      crm: updateCrmRecord,
      schedule: scheduleAppointment,
      outboundCall: placeOutboundCall,
    },
  });
  await saveConversationState(from, agentResult.updatedState);
  if (agentResult.smsToSend) {
    await sendSmsViaTwilio({
      to: from,
      body: agentResult.smsToSend,
    });
  }
  res.status(200).send("OK");
}

The only difference between voice and SMS here is:

  • Voice has audio perception + audio action layers.
  • SMS is text-in, text-out.

The agent logic is identical.

That’s the power of agentic architecture: interface-agnostic intelligence.

Tool Design: Why Tools Matter More Than Prompts

In agentic systems, prompts matter but tools matter more.

Tools define what the agent can do, not just what it can say.

In this system, typical tools include:

  • sendSms(to, body)
  • updateCrmRecord(userId, fields)
  • scheduleAppointment(userId, datetime)
  • placeOutboundCall(phoneNumber, context)
  • logEvent(type, payload)
  • escalateToHuman(callSid)

The agent’s job is not to talk it’s to decide which tools to use and when.

That’s how you get:

  • Voice → CRM → SMS → Outbound call → Resolution
  • Without hard-coded flows
  • Without brittle logic trees

Why Twilio + LiveKit Is the Right Stack for Real-Time Voice Agents

Let’s talk about why this specific combination works so well.

Why Twilio

Twilio provides:

  • Global phone numbers
  • Carrier-grade telephony reliability
  • Inbound + outbound call handling
  • SMS/MMS
  • SIP trunking
  • Call routing
  • Call control APIs

It’s the telephony substrate.

You don’t replace Twilio you build intelligence on top of it.

Why LiveKit

LiveKit solves the hardest problem in real-time AI voice systems:

Low-latency bidirectional audio streaming.

It provides:

  • WebRTC-grade audio transport
  • Sub-100 ms media latency
  • Audio track control
  • Real-time audio events
  • Barge-in detection hooks
  • Server-side audio pipelines

Twilio can get you the call.

LiveKit can get you real-time conversational control.

Together, they let you build:

  • Real-time inbound voice agents
  • Outbound AI calling systems
  • Streaming speech pipelines
  • Interruptible, human-like conversations

This combination is what makes real-time voice AI agents practical instead of theoretical.

STT, TTS, and LLM Stack Considerations (Production Reality)

Let’s talk briefly about model choices not as vendor marketing, but as engineering tradeoffs.

Speech-to-Text (STT)

Common production choices:

  • Whisper
  • Pros: strong accuracy, multilingual
  • Cons: slower unless optimized, harder to stream at scale
  • Deepgram
  • Pros: excellent streaming latency, robust diarization
  • Cons: sometimes less accurate on domain jargon
  • AssemblyAI
  • Pros: strong enterprise features, good streaming APIs
  • Cons: slightly higher latency depending on model

In real-time voice agents, latency beats raw accuracy past a threshold.

I prefer streaming-first STT models under ~200 ms partial latency.

Text-to-Speech (TTS)

Common production choices:

  • ElevenLabs
  • Pros: extremely natural voices
  • Cons: synthesis latency varies by voice
  • Azure Neural TTS
  • Pros: fast, stable, enterprise-grade
  • Cons: slightly less expressive
  • Google Cloud TTS
  • Pros: reliable, fast
  • Cons: voice quality slightly behind ElevenLabs

For real-time agents, consistent sub-150 ms synthesis matters more than perfect emotional tone.

LLMs

Common choices:

  • OpenAI GPT-4.x
  • Pros: strong reasoning, tool calling
  • Cons: latency variance, cost
  • Anthropic Claude
  • Pros: long context, strong instruction following
  • Cons: slightly slower at times

In agentic systems, the LLM is not a chatbot it’s a planner.

You want:

  • Reliable tool calling
  • Stable reasoning
  • Predictable latency
  • Strong instruction adherence

Model selection matters less than architecture discipline.

The Biggest Mistake Teams Make: Treating Voice AI Like Chat

Most failures I see in Twilio voice AI agent systems come from one mistake:

Treating voice like chat with audio I/O.

Voice is not chat.

Voice is:

  • Continuous
  • Interruptible
  • Time-sensitive
  • Emotionally expressive
  • Latency-intolerant
  • Context-fragile

If your architecture assumes:

  • Turn boundaries are clean
  • Users won’t interrupt
  • Latency is flexible
  • State can live in the prompt
  • Responses can wait for full generation

Your system will fail in production.

Agentic voice systems require:

  • Real-time loops
  • Cancelable actions
  • Explicit state management
  • Streaming pipelines
  • Observability-first design

This is systems engineering, not prompt engineering.

Scaling Beyond Demos: Production Hardening Checklist

If you’re building a real Twilio voice AI agent or LiveKit voice automation system, here’s what separates production systems from prototypes:

Latency

  • Streaming STT
  • Token-streaming LLMs
  • Incremental TTS playback
  • Regional co-location

Barge-in

  • Real-time audio energy detection
  • TTS cancellation
  • Agent plan invalidation
  • Priority reprocessing

State

  • Centralized conversation store
  • Cross-channel continuity
  • Explicit tool-side effects
  • Session recovery

Observability

  • End-to-end tracing
  • Latency metrics
  • Tool failure logs
  • Conversation transcripts
  • Business outcome metrics

Safety & Reliability

  • Human escalation paths
  • Fallback responses
  • Rate limiting
  • Error recovery
  • Abuse detection

This is what it takes to ship real-time voice agents that survive production traffic.

Why This Architecture Scales Beyond Support Bots

Once you build this correctly, you’re no longer building “voice bots.”

You’re building:

  • AI call center agents
  • Automated appointment schedulers
  • Voice-based onboarding flows
  • AI sales callers
  • Healthcare intake agents
  • Real-time customer success agents
  • Outbound collections agents
  • Multilingual support systems

Because the agent is not scripted it’s goal-driven.

And voice + SMS become just interfaces to a general intelligence layer.

  • Perceive → Reason → Act loop
  • Tools branching off the agent
  • Voice and SMS as interfaces
  • State store at center

The Strategic Shift: From Flows to Systems

This project fundamentally changed how I think about automation.

I no longer design:

  • IVR trees
  • Dialogue graphs
  • State machines
  • Scripted flows

I design:

  • Goals
  • Tools
  • Constraints
  • State models
  • Latency budgets
  • Recovery paths

And then I let the agent operate inside those boundaries.

Instead of:

“If user says X, do Y.”

It becomes:

“Given this user’s situation and goal, what’s the best next action?”

That shift turns voice systems from:

  • Reactive → proactive
  • Scripted → adaptive
  • Brittle → resilient
  • Channel-bound → channel-agnostic

This is what agentic AI pipelines actually enable.

Why Twilio + LiveKit Is Becoming the Default Stack for Voice AI Agents

In practice, I’ve found:

  • Twilio solves the telephony problem better than anyone else.
  • LiveKit solves the real-time media problem better than anyone else.
  • LLMs solve the reasoning problem.
  • Agentic architectures solve the workflow problem.

Together, they unlock:

  • Real-time voice AI agents
  • Interruptible conversations
  • Multi-step workflows
  • Cross-channel continuity
  • Outbound AI calling
  • Human-like interactions at scale

That’s why we’re seeing more teams move from:

“Chatbot with a phone number”

to:

“Voice-native agentic systems.”

Final Thoughts: This Isn’t About Voice It’s About Control

Agentic AI isn’t a UI upgrade.

It’s a control architecture upgrade.

Instead of building systems that respond to inputs, we’re building systems that:

  • Maintain goals
  • Track progress
  • Adapt to interruptions
  • Take initiative
  • Operate continuously

Twilio and LiveKit make it possible to bring that architecture into real-time voice and SMS, where latency, interruptions, and human expectations are unforgiving.

In this article, I’ve walked through:

  • Why traditional IVR and chatbot systems fail in modern voice environments
  • What an agentic AI pipeline actually looks like in production
  • How Twilio + LiveKit enable real-time voice automation at scale
  • The real engineering challenges: latency, barge-in, state, observability
  • Concrete pseudo-code for building these systems
  • Architecture patterns you can deploy immediately

Next, I’m benchmarking:

  • Different STT/TTS stacks under real call load
  • Alternative agent planning architectures
  • Memory and state modeling strategies
  • Observability and recovery patterns

And I’ll turn that into deeper implementation guides with:

  • Reference architectures
  • Open-source templates
  • Performance benchmarks
  • Failure case studies

Because real-time voice AI isn’t about demos.

It’s about building systems that survive production traffic, angry users, interruptions, latency spikes, and edge cases and still deliver outcomes.

That’s what agentic pipelines enable.

And that’s why I no longer build scripts.

I build agents.
